findings.issue_text: [BUG] The login form resolves through zodResolver(formSchema), which this diff never extends with backupCode, and zod's default unknown-key stripping removes the registered backupCode field from the values handed to the submit handler, so signIn("credentials") is invoked without backupCode. A user who clicks 'Lost access' and submits a valid backup code gets a silent no-op: the credential never reaches next-auth's authorize, the totpCode branch throws SecondFactorRequired, and the handler only re-sets twoFactorRequired without rendering any message — backup-code login is completely non-functional, and the e2e TODO in this same PR leaves exactly this path untested.

[BUG] The enable-success path replaces the immediate onEnable() with setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes), leaving the backup-codes 'close' button as the only code path that calls onEnable() and resetState(). A user who presses Esc (or any onOpenChange dismissal) at the backup-codes step closes the dialog with onEnable never fired: the settings toggle keeps showing 2FA disabled while the account is actually enabled, and reopening the modal resumes at the stale backup-codes step — codes dismissed without downloading are gone permanently because the diff ships no re-view or regeneration path.

[BUG] The missing_backup_codes message tells users to 'generate them in your settings', but this diff ships no settings path that creates backup codes for an account that already has 2FA enabled — the setup endpoint only runs inside the enable flow. Every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy (their backupCodes column is null) and any user who consumed all 10 codes hits this dead end after losing their authenticator: the error points at a feature that does not exist, and the only real recovery — disabling 2FA — itself requires the TOTP code they no longer have.

[BUG] The diff adds a FIXME admitting the assertion is broken instead of fixing it: expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy() passes an unawaited Promise<boolean> to expect(), and a Promise object is always truthy, so the check can never fail. The '2FA is enabled' verification in this e2e test is a no-op, so a regression that leaves 2FA disabled after the enable flow still passes CI; the fix is `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]')).toBeChecked()`.

[BUG] The missing-CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY guard throws new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError) inside the Next.js API handler instead of returning res.status(500).json({ error }) like every other failure in this route. On a server without the encryption key the disable route responds with an unhandled 500 whose body is not the { error } JSON the modal parses, so the client falls through to the generic 'something_went_wrong' and the operator gets an uncaught-exception log instead of the route's own error contract.

[ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component's default export is declared as `function TwoFactor`, a copy-paste of the TOTP component's name. React DevTools, crash stack traces, and grep now show two unrelated auth components both named TwoFactor, so the next person debugging 2FA lands in the wrong file and misreads traces that actually point at the backup-code input.

[ADVISORY] The download control nests a <Button> inside an <a> element, which the HTML content model forbids (an anchor must contain no interactive content). Screen readers expose two interactive elements for a single action and the markup fails HTML validation; because the sibling copy/close buttons already call e.preventDefault(), the next refactor that adds a preventDefault-ing onClick to this Button silently kills the download.

[ADVISORY] The copy button calls navigator.clipboard.writeText unguarded, and the Clipboard API is undefined on non-secure origins. Self-hosted cal.com instances served over plain HTTP (intranet installs) get a dead button: the onClick throws a TypeError, no success toast appears, and the codes are never copied.

[ADVISORY] The cancel path never resets twoFactorLostAccess or clears errorMessage — resetForm and setTwoFactorLostAccess(false) are wired only to the lost-access toggle and the success handler, not to onCancel. A user who switches to 'Lost access', hits an error, and cancels reopens the disable modal still in backup-code mode with the stale error rendered, unlike the sibling EnableTwoFactorModal whose cancel button calls resetState().

[BUG] The login page never transmits the backup code: the diff adds the BackupCode input, the LoginValues.backupCode field, and handling for IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes responses, but no hunk adds backupCode to the signIn('credentials') payload or to the zod formSchema behind zodResolver, so the submitted credentials contain no backupCode and the server's backup-code branch is unreachable from login. A user who lost their authenticator switches to 'Lost access', enters a valid backup code, and the credentials request goes out without it; the server takes the TOTP branch and returns SecondFactorRequired, which the handler answers by only re-setting twoFactorRequired(true) with no visible message, so the user is silently locked out despite holding valid codes — the sibling disable flow did get its payload updated in TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable, which is exactly the wiring missed here.

[BUG] During the DisplayBackupCodes step the cancel button is removed and onEnable/resetState are wired only into the Close button, leaving every other dismissal path (ESC, the DialogContent close X, overlay click through onOpenChange) with no onEnable or resetState call. 2FA is already enabled server-side at this step, so a user who dismisses the dialog any way other than the Close button returns to settings with the switch still showing 2FA disabled until a full refresh, and reopening the modal resumes at the stale DisplayBackupCodes step displaying the previous session's codes because resetState never ran.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises backup-code authentication: the new verification/consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts, the backup branch in disable.ts, and both lost-access UI toggles ship with zero coverage, and the added TODO at the top of this file admits it. A regression in code consumption (wrong index nulled, failed re-encrypt) or in the request wiring ships green — the missing-payload defect in login.tsx in this very PR is precisely the class of bug this gap lets through, and users end up locked out or codes reusable with no failing test.

[ADVISORY] The missing_backup_codes string instructs users to 'generate them in your settings', but the diff adds no settings path that generates backup codes — the only writer is the setup endpoint inside the enable flow — so existing 2FA users (backupCodes null after the migration) have no way to obtain codes without first disabling 2FA. A pre-existing 2FA user who lost their authenticator follows the message to a feature that does not exist; they cannot produce backup codes and cannot disable 2FA without the TOTP they lost (the disable modal's lost-access path returns the same dead end), so the lockout this PR was meant to rescue persists while the UI actively misdirects them.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a FIXME documenting that expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy() passes even when the two-factor switch is unchecked, but leaves the vacuous assertion in place instead of replacing it with the data-state check the sibling test below uses. The primary 2FA-enable e2e test gives false assurance about the switch state, so enable-flow regressions — like the onEnable-skipping dismissal path added in this same diff — pass CI undetected.

[ADVISORY] The download and copy tests assert only the suggested filename and the success toast; the in-diff TODOs concede that the backup codes' actual content is never verified on either path. A regression in formatBackupCode or in the blob/clipboard text (wrong slicing, missing codes, wrong join) keeps the suite green while users save a garbled or empty codes file and only discover it during lockout recovery.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are displayed exactly once with no re-view path (the diff adds no endpoint to read stored codes; they are only regenerated by a full disable-and-re-enable cycle) and neither the step UI nor backup_code_instructions warns that the codes will not be shown again. A user who closes the dialog without copying or downloading permanently loses access to their codes without realizing it and is locked out when the authenticator is later lost — the standard save-these-now acceptance criterion for backup-code UX is absent.

[BUG] tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes the control from the keyboard tab order, making the show/hide button unreachable and unactivatable by keyboard in every PasswordField. Keyboard-only and assistive-tech users can no longer reveal a masked password anywhere the shared PasswordField renders — including the new 2FA password and backup-code flows — a WCAG 2.1.1 regression on a shared component.

[ADVISORY] The only input normalization on the backup-code path is dash-stripping: the indexOf comparison is case- and whitespace-sensitive, with no trim or case folding on either the server compare or the BackupCode TextField, whose uppercase placeholder 'XXXXX-XXXXX' invites exactly the uppercase typing that fails. A code typed with mobile auto-capitalization (or pasted with surrounding whitespace) fails with incorrect_backup_code despite being valid, burning the user's recovery attempt at the moment they are locked out.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write: authorize decrypts the list, nulls the matched index, and writes the whole re-encrypted list back with no transaction, lock, or atomic update, so concurrent logins race on the stale list. Two simultaneous logins with the same code both succeed (one code grants two sessions), and two simultaneous logins with different codes lose one consumption to the last writer, resurrecting a spent code — both violate the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' promise the UI displays.

[ADVISORY] The disable endpoint's backup-code comparison repeats the normalization gap: indexOf on the raw user string with only dash-stripping, no trim or case folding, while the UI placeholder suggests uppercase codes. A user disabling 2FA via a lost-access backup code typed in uppercase or with stray whitespace gets incorrect_backup_code for a valid code and cannot complete the disable flow.

[ADVISORY] The decrypt-and-indexOf backup-code verification is hand-duplicated between this endpoint and the credentials authorize in next-auth-options.ts, with intentional behavioral drift between the copies (login consumes the matched code, disable does not) and no shared helper. The next change to verification semantics — trim/case normalization, constant-time compare, or an atomicity fix — must be applied in two places, and the drift already present means one path silently diverges and accepts or rejects codes differently than the other.

[ADVISORY] The visible 'Backup Code' Label carries no htmlFor and the TextField is passed label='', so the backup-code input renders with no programmatic accessible name. Screen-reader users reaching the lost-access recovery field hear an unlabeled edit box identified only by placeholder, at the step where they are already locked out and most need accessible guidance.

[ADVISORY] BackupCode.tsx default-exports a function still named TwoFactor, a copy-paste leftover that leaves two distinct components named TwoFactor under components/auth. React DevTools, stack traces, and a grep for 'function TwoFactor' present the backup-code UI as TwoFactor, so the next developer debugging or extending backup codes reads or patches the wrong file.

[BUG] The diff widens LoginValues with backupCode and registers a backupCode input, but never adds backupCode to the zod formSchema that zodResolver uses and never touches the signIn('credentials') call, so zod's default strip mode removes the field from the values handed to the submit handler and the backup code is never transmitted to the server. A user who clicks 'lost access' and enters a valid backup code gets SecondFactorRequired/incorrect-2fa errors instead of a session — the login recovery path, the headline of this feature, never works; the diff's own TODO confirms no test exercises backup-code login, so this ships undetected.

[BUG] Backup codes are provisioned only inside the enable flow (setup.ts), so every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy has backupCodes=null, yet login.tsx unconditionally offers them the 'lost access' path and the resulting MissingBackupCodes error tells them to 'generate them in your settings' — a regeneration surface that exists nowhere in this diff. Pre-existing 2FA users who lose their authenticator are funneled into a recovery UI that always fails and an instruction pointing at a nonexistent settings control; the only regeneration path is disable+re-enable, which itself requires a working second factor, so they remain locked out.

[BUG] onEnable() was moved from TOTP-verification success to the backup-codes screen's Close button, so dismissing the dialog through its native close path (X/Esc via onOpenChange) at the DisplayBackupCodes step never calls onEnable or resetState. The parent settings UI keeps showing 2FA disabled while it is enabled server-side; when the user retries, setup.ts regenerates and overwrites backupCodes and the TOTP secret, silently invalidating the codes they just downloaded and their authenticator entry.

[BUG] The copy button fires showToast('backup_codes_copied') synchronously after navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting it, and navigator.clipboard is undefined on non-secure origins. A rejected writeText (permission denied) still shows 'Backup codes copied!' and a self-hosted user on HTTP gets a silently dead button — either way the user closes the dialog believing their only recovery codes are saved when the clipboard is empty.

[ADVISORY] The only backup-code tests added exercise the display step (download filename, copy toast, close button); the security-critical paths — authorize() verification and single-use consumption in next-auth-options.ts and backup-code disable in disable.ts — have zero coverage, as the diff's own TODO ('add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') admits. A regression that stops consuming used codes (breaking the 'exactly once' invariant the UI copy promises) or breaks backup login/disabled-2FA-via-backup entirely merges green because the e2e suite never touches those paths.

[ADVISORY] The PR adds tabIndex={-1} to the shared PasswordField visibility toggle in packages/ui — an app-wide keyboard-navigation change untraceable to the backup-codes feature. Every password field in the app loses its Tab-reachable show/hide toggle, and the behavior change ships untested as a rider on a 2FA PR, so any keyboard-accessibility regression it causes is mis-attributed to the backup-codes work.

[ADVISORY] The new BackupCode component's default export is declared as `export default function TwoFactor(...)`, copy-pasted from TwoFactor.tsx. React DevTools, the profiler, and error-boundary/stack-trace output label the backup-code input 'TwoFactor', misleading anyone debugging the lost-access lockout flow and sending symbol greps for TwoFactor into the wrong file.

[ADVISORY] EnableTwoFactorModal's cancel path got resetState() wired in this same diff, but DisableTwoFactorModal's cancel leaves twoFactorLostAccess=true — only the toggle handler resets fields, never the cancel path. A user who clicks 'lost access', cancels, and later reopens the disable modal finds it already in backup-code mode with the TOTP input gone and must discover the 'go back' toggle to reach the expected flow.

[ADVISORY] The decrypt→normalize→indexOf backup-code verification block is hand-duplicated between this endpoint and next-auth-options.ts, with already-divergent consumption semantics (login nulls the used code; disable leaves it for the later wipe-all). The next change to verification (hashing codes at rest, adding attempt limits) must be applied in both files; updating only the login copy leaves the disable endpoint — which removes the barrier protecting the account — on the weaker path.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write (decrypt, null the matched index, update the whole array), so two concurrent logins race and the second update resurrects codes the first already consumed. A stolen code can be replayed in parallel to obtain multiple sessions from one code, and an already-used code re-enters the valid set — the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' promise displayed in the UI is not enforced under concurrency.

[BUG] The login flow never transmits the backup code to the server: the diff registers the backupCode form field and renders the BackupCode input, but leaves both the zod formSchema and the signIn() invocation untouched, so zodResolver strips backupCode from the submitted values and credentials.backupCode is always undefined in authorize(). A user who has lost their authenticator clicks 'lost access', enters a valid backup code, and submits; the request carries only email/password (totpCode was cleared), authorize() falls into the plain twoFactorEnabled branch, throws SecondFactorRequired, and the user sees '2fa required' — the backup-code login feature, the PR's core purpose, is unreachable and the user remains locked out.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is an unguarded read-modify-write on user.backupCodes (decrypt, indexOf, null the element, prisma.user.update) with no optimistic-concurrency version, transaction, or conditional update. Two concurrent sign-ins presenting the same backup code both read the same list, both match, and both receive sessions — the single-use invariant the UI promises ('Each backup code can be used exactly once') is not enforced; concurrent use of two different codes also resurrects an already-consumed code via last-write-wins.

[BUG] onEnable() is deferred from the successful enable response to the backup-codes 'close' footer button, so dismissing the dialog at the DisplayBackupCodes step through its built-in close affordances (X button, Escape, outside click → onOpenChange) never notifies the parent that 2FA was enabled. A user who closes the backup-codes dialog with Escape or the X leaves the settings page showing the 2FA switch unchecked while the server has 2FA enabled (and never saved the codes), leaving the parent UI stale and the user uncertain whether enablement succeeded until a full refresh.

[ADVISORY] The new MissingBackupCodes copy tells users to 'generate them in your settings', but the diff implements no settings UI or API to view, regenerate, or create backup codes for an account that already has 2FA enabled — the only generator (totp/setup) runs during initial enablement and the modal shows the codes exactly once. Every user who enabled 2FA before this migration (backupCodes is null) and every user who loses their printed codes hits this message at the exact moment they are locked out, and the instruction is impossible to follow: getting into settings requires a login, and the only regeneration path is disabling 2FA, which itself requires a working TOTP code.

[ADVISORY] The e2e suite exercises only the backup-codes display step (download/copy/close) and explicitly defers 'login + disabling 2fa with backup' to a TODO, so both new server-side verification paths (the authorize() backup branch and the disable route's backup branch) ship with zero coverage. The suite stays green while the login backup-code path is in fact broken (see the login.tsx finding) — exactly the green-CI/red-production case the TODO acknowledges; any regression in the consume-once logic or either verification branch ships undetected.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code verification logic (encryption-key guard, symmetricDecrypt, dash-strip, indexOf) is copy-pasted between this route and authorize() in next-auth-options.ts instead of a shared helper, and the two copies already diverge: the login path consumes the matched code while the disable path does not. The next normalization change (case-folding, trimming, format change) applied to one copy but not the other makes a code accepted at login but rejected at disable (or vice versa), silently splitting the two flows that users expect to behave identically.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code format is encoded as unlinked magic numbers across three files — crypto.randomBytes(5) here (10 hex chars), minLength 10/maxLength 11 in BackupCode.tsx, and slice(0,5)/slice(5,10) in formatBackupCode — with no shared constant or named length. Changing the generator (e.g. randomBytes(6)) compiles cleanly but formatBackupCode silently truncates the displayed and downloaded codes so users save codes that can never match the stored ones, and the client's maxLength rejects valid input — a lockout manufactured by copy divergence.

[ADVISORY] authorize() persists the consumed backup code (nulls it and rewrites the row) before the rest of the sign-in pipeline runs, so the single-use code is burned even when sign-in subsequently fails. A user whose authorize() call throws after the 2FA block (e.g. an organization SSO redirect or any later check) permanently loses one of their 10 codes per attempt without ever receiving a session, and can exhaust all codes into the MissingBackupCodes dead end.

[ADVISORY] BackupCode.tsx's default export is declared as `export default function TwoFactor`, duplicating the name of the pre-existing TwoFactor component it is imported beside in login.tsx and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx. React DevTools, error stack traces, and fast-refresh all identify the backup-code input as 'TwoFactor', and a developer grepping `function TwoFactor` or refactoring imports binds the wrong component — the confusable pair is already mounted in the same files.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are stored as lowercase hex (crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')) but verification compares raw user input with a case-sensitive indexOf and no lowercasing, while the BackupCode input sets no autoCapitalize/autoCorrect guard. A user hand-transcribing a code from the printed/downloaded sheet in uppercase (typical on autocapitalizing mobile keyboards) is told 'Backup code is incorrect' for a valid code while locked out of their account.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are generated and persisted at setup time but displayed after enable from the setup response held in React state, with no server-side binding between the codes shown and the codes actually stored. If setup runs again in another tab or session between this tab's setup and enable (each setup call regenerates and overwrites the stored codes), the modal displays and lets the user download the now-stale first set, which the server will reject at every future login.

[ADVISORY] The password-visibility toggle button in PasswordField is given tabIndex={-1}, removing it from keyboard tab order in every form that renders a PasswordField (login, 2FA enable, 2FA disable). Keyboard-only users can no longer reveal their password on any of these forms — the control becomes mouse-only, an accessibility regression relative to the pre-existing tabbable behavior.

[BUG] The login page never transmits the backupCode value to the credentials endpoint: the zod formSchema is never updated to include the new field (zodResolver strips unknown keys before the submit handler sees them), and the request body constructed in signIn — the unchanged region between this diff's hunks, written before backupCode existed — enumerates only the pre-existing credentials, so authorize() in next-auth-options.ts always takes the TOTP branch and throws SecondFactorRequired. A user who lost their authenticator clicks 'Lost access', enters a valid backup code, and submits: no error message appears and no login occurs (SecondFactorRequired just re-sets the already-visible 2FA state), so the PR's headline recovery flow is dead on the login page and the newly added IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes handlers at login.tsx:157-158 are unreachable dead code.

[BUG] onEnable() now fires only from the 'Close' button's onClick on the DisplayBackupCodes step (the Cancel button is hidden at that step), so dismissing the dialog via ESC, the X button, or overlay click — which route through onOpenChange — completes the enable server-side without ever notifying the parent. The parent settings UI keeps rendering 2FA as disabled after a successful enable; when the user 're-enables', setup.ts regenerates and overwrites the stored backupCodes, silently invalidating the codes the user just downloaded — the saved file then fails with IncorrectBackupCode at the exact lost-access login it was saved for.

[BUG] The 'Each backup code can be used exactly once' guarantee (stated verbatim in the new backup_code_instructions locale string) is enforced with a non-atomic read–null–rewrite: authorize() decrypts the array and indexOf-matches the code, then rewrites the entire array via prisma.user.update with no transaction, row lock, or compare-and-swap. Two concurrent sign-ins presenting the same backup code both pass indexOf and both receive sessions (code used twice), and two concurrent sign-ins with different codes race the whole-array rewrite so last-write-wins resurrects the loser's already-consumed code — on serverless (independent invocations, shared DB) nothing serializes them, breaking the single-use constraint the artifact itself promises.

[BUG] The copy handler calls navigator.clipboard.writeText() fire-and-forget and unconditionally fires the success toast on the next line, with no await, no catch, and no fallback. On insecure origins (self-hosted cal.com served over plain http) navigator.clipboard is undefined, so the click throws a TypeError with zero feedback; on a clipboard-permission rejection in a secure context the 'Backup codes copied!' toast has already fired, assuring the user their only recovery secrets are in the clipboard when they are not.

[ADVISORY] The two new security-critical server flows — backup-code verification plus single-use consumption in authorize() and the backup-code branch in totp/disable.ts — ship with zero test coverage, as the diff's own TODO ('add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup') admits. The broken login-page transmission (backupCode never reaches the server) and any consumption regression (e.g., failing to null the used code, silently voiding exactly-once) pass CI green; the e2e suite exercises only the enable-and-display happy path, so the next contributor gets no signal when these paths break.

[BUG] The missing_backup_codes message instructs users to 'Please generate them in your settings', but this diff adds no settings UI, endpoint, or action that generates or regenerates backup codes — the only writer is the setup endpoint reached during initial enable. Every user who enabled 2FA before this deploy (backupCodes is null after the migration) is told to perform an impossible action; their real path is disable-then-re-enable 2FA, and a user hitting this error at the login screen cannot reach settings at all — the message misdirects exactly the users the feature exists to rescue.

[BUG] The diff ships the author's own FIXME acknowledging the switch assertion is vacuous — expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy() always passes because isChecked() returns a Promise (a truthy object) even when the switch is unchecked — instead of fixing it to the data-state="checked" check the sibling test uses. The suite green-lies about enablement being reflected in the settings UI; the onEnable-only-on-Close regression (ESC dismissal leaving the switch stale) is precisely what this assertion exists to catch and cannot, so it will never fail regardless of what breaks.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code verification block (encryption-key guard, symmetricDecrypt, JSON.parse, dash-strip, indexOf) is duplicated verbatim between authorize() in next-auth-options.ts and this disable endpoint, with copy-paste drift already visible: disable.ts logs 'cannot proceed with backup code login' while serving a disable request. The next change to code format or verification (hashing at rest, code length, dash handling) must be replicated in two security-critical auth entry points; updating one leaves the other accepting stale-format codes, and an operator triaging a failed disable sees a log that blames 'login'.

[ADVISORY] BackupCode.tsx declares its default export as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })` — a copy-paste of the sibling TwoFactor.tsx — leaving two distinct components in the codebase both named TwoFactor. React DevTools, the profiler, and stack traces label the lost-access backup-code input 'TwoFactor', and grepping for a BackupCode component finds no function of that name, sending the next person debugging the login flow to the wrong component and file.

[BUG] The diff registers a backupCode field on the login form and adds it to the LoginValues type, but never adds backupCode to the zod formSchema that zodResolver uses, so zod strips the key from the parsed values handleSubmit delivers to handleFormSubmit and the backup code is never transmitted to signIn("credentials"). A user who lost their authenticator submits a valid backup code and the login silently no-ops: the request goes out with email+password only, the server answers SecondFactorRequired, the client re-sets twoFactorRequired (already true) and renders no error, and the user loops forever and stays locked out of their account despite holding a valid recovery code — the headline feature of this PR is dead on the login page (the disable modal works only because it uses useForm without a resolver, and the e2e TODO defers exactly this test).

[ADVISORY] The new MissingBackupCodes path tells users to "generate them in your settings", but this diff creates no code-generation path for an account that already has twoFactorEnabled set — backup codes are only minted inside the enable flow's setup call — so the instruction points at a flow that does not exist. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature (backupCodes is null for all of them after the migration) and then loses their authenticator hits a dead end: they cannot generate codes without disabling 2FA, and disabling requires the TOTP or a backup code they do not have, so the recovery feature is unusable for exactly the locked-out population it exists to save, while the message misleads them and support.

[BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-match-null-write (indexOf against the decrypted array, then an unconditional prisma.user.update of the whole array) with no transaction or conditional update, so two concurrent sign-in requests submitting the same code both pass indexOf before either persists the null. A single backup code authenticates two sessions, violating the exactly-once guarantee the UI states ("Each backup code can be used exactly once"); a code leaked once (clipboard manager, shoulder-surfing, screenshot) can be replayed concurrently with the legitimate use and both attempts succeed.

[BUG] req.body.backupCode is gated only by a truthiness check (line 48) and then used as req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""), which throws a TypeError when the client sends a non-string JSON value such as 123, true, or {}. A single crafted POST to /api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable with a non-string backupCode produces an unhandled exception and a 500 instead of the 4xx the endpoint's error contract promises, bypassing the IncorrectBackupCode handling and giving an attacker a trivially triggered server-error path on an auth endpoint.

[BUG] credentials.backupCode is used without any type check and credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "") throws a TypeError when the credentials request carries a non-string backupCode value. The next-auth credentials callback for that request fails with an unhandled TypeError surfaced as a generic sign-in error instead of the clean IncorrectBackupCode rejection, so the new authentication path crashes on malformed input rather than rejecting it with the error code the client is built to display.

[BUG] The backup code is verified with Array.prototype.indexOf, whose === comparison short-circuits at the first differing character, so the login response time leaks how many leading characters of the submitted code match a stored code instead of comparing the secret in constant time. Unlike a 30-second TOTP token, backup codes are long-lived secrets, so a co-located or low-jitter attacker who already holds the victim's password gets a per-request prefix-match oracle that prunes the 40-bit search space character by character; hashing both sides and comparing with crypto.timingSafeEqual closes it in one line.

[BUG] The disable endpoint verifies the backup code with Array.prototype.indexOf, whose === comparison short-circuits at the first differing character, leaking partial-match information through response timing instead of comparing the secret in constant time. An attacker who already holds the victim's password (the password check runs before this branch) can use response-time differences to prune the backup-code search space character by character on a second endpoint that accepts the same long-lived secret.

[ADVISORY] Backup codes are verification-only, one-time secrets that nothing ever needs to read back except an equality check, yet they are stored with reversible symmetric encryption under the app-wide CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY instead of a salted hash. Compromise of the single CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY (or any code path holding it) decrypts every user's unused backup codes in one pass; unlike TOTP secrets, which must be recoverable to compute HMACs, backup codes could be hashed like passwords and remain useless to an attacker even under key compromise, so the chosen storage strictly widens the blast radius of the most damaging key in the system.

[ADVISORY] The Dialog passes onOpenChange straight to the parent, so ESC, backdrop click, or the DialogContent X closes the modal at any step, and nothing prevents closing during the new DisplayBackupCodes step — the only place the codes are ever shown. A user who enables 2FA and then dismisses the dialog with ESC or the X instead of the Close button ends up with 2FA enabled and backup codes that were never displayed; since this diff ships no retrieval or regeneration path, the codes are effectively lost and the user believes they hold a recovery option that does not exist — the harm surfaces exactly when they later lose the authenticator.

[ADVISORY] The backup-code verification routine (decrypt, dash-strip, indexOf match) is hand-duplicated between this endpoint and the login authorize() in next-auth-options.ts, and the two copies have already drifted: login consumes the used code by nulling and re-encrypting, while this copy relies on the trailing backupCodes:null wipe. The next hardening applied to one copy — constant-time comparison, hashed storage, or a normalization change — silently leaves the other authentication path on the weaker behavior, and the disable copy's non-consumption is one refactor away from becoming a code-replay bug if the trailing wipe is ever reorganized.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx` the PR adds `backupCode` to `LoginValues` and renders `<BackupCode />` registered as `methods.register("backupCode")`, plus UI to switch to the lost-access flow. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup-code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write — JSON.parse of the encrypted blob, nulling one entry, then an unconditional prisma.user.update — with no transaction, row lock, or version guard, so concurrent sign-ins overwrite each other's writes. Two overlapping sign-in attempts (double-submit, two tabs, a retry racing the first request) both pass the indexOf check against the same snapshot: the same code authenticates twice, and the later write restores a code the earlier request already consumed, silently breaking the 'each backup code can be used exactly once' invariant the UI promises.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts`, backup-code consumption is implemented as a read/validate/write sequence: decrypt+`JSON.parse` the stored `user.backupCodes`, `indexOf` the provided code, then set `backupCodes[index] = null` and persist via an unconditional `prisma.user.update` (re-encrypting the whole array). There’s no transaction, conditional update, or optimistic locking to prevent two concurrent authorize calls from both validating against the same snapshot and both succeeding, violating the “use exactly once” invariant and potentially overwriting each other’s consumed-code updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The missing-encryption-key guard throws `new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError)` inside the API handler instead of returning res.status(500).json({ error }) like every other error path in this endpoint and like setup.ts's identical guard. When CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is absent (misconfigured deploy), the endpoint returns Next.js's non-JSON 500, the client's `await response.json()` throws, and the user falls to the generic something-went-wrong path while the operator loses the structured error envelope every other failure here provides.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the new backup-code path checks `if (!process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY) { ...; throw new Error(ErrorCode.InternalServerError); }` instead of returning a JSON error response like the other branches in this handler (which use `return res.status(400).json({ error: ... })`). An uncaught `throw` in a Next.js API route will produce a generic 500 response (often non-JSON), which can break callers that do `await response.json()` (e.g., `DisableTwoFactorModal` reads `await response.json()` on non-200 responses). This leads to inconsistent/broken client error handling and loss of the structured `{ error }` envelope.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The lost-access login flow never transmits the backup code to the server: this diff adds backupCode to the LoginValues interface and registers the field via the BackupCode component, but the zod formSchema and the signIn('credentials') call are both unchanged, so zodResolver strips the schema-unknown backupCode key from the values handleSubmit passes to handleSignIn and the credentials request goes out without it. authorize() falls into the TOTP branch, sees credentials.totpCode empty (it is cleared when switching to the lost-access view), and throws SecondFactorRequired; the login page's handler for that code only re-sets twoFactorRequired(true) and renders no message, so a user who lost their authenticator enters a backup code, clicks Sign in, and nothing visibly happens — backup-code login is dead and the failure is invisible.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows LoginValues gained `backupCode` and the UI can register it via the new `BackupCode` component, but the finding’s core claim depends on code not present in the diff: (1) the contents/behavior of `formSchema` (whether it includes `backupCode` or uses `.passthrough()`), and (2) how `handleSignIn`/`signIn('credentials')` constructs the credentials payload. Without seeing those, we can’t verify that zodResolver strips `backupCode` or that the request omits it. The login page also adds error handling for `IncorrectBackupCode`/`MissingBackupCodes`, suggesting the flow may be wired elsewhere.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The copy button fires navigator.clipboard.writeText without awaiting it and shows the 'Backup codes copied!' success toast synchronously before the write completes, with no rejection handler. When the clipboard write rejects (permission denied, embedded/unfocused document) the user still sees the success toast while the clipboard is empty; since backup codes are displayed exactly once with no retrieval path, the user closes the dialog and permanently loses codes they believe they copied — and on insecure origins navigator.clipboard is undefined, so the click throws a TypeError with no feedback at all.

adjudication.rationale: In `EnableTwoFactorModal.tsx`, the copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without `await`/`.then` and immediately calls `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")` (see the `data-testid="backup-codes-copy"` button). There is no rejection handling, so a failed clipboard write (permissions/unfocused/unsupported) still shows a success toast. Additionally, if `navigator.clipboard` is undefined (e.g., insecure context), `navigator.clipboard.writeText` will throw at click time and there is no catch/feedback. This is a concrete broken behavior introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] handleEnable's success path replaces the immediate onEnable() call with setStep(DisplayBackupCodes), deferring the parent's onEnable callback to that step's Close button, but the dialog's own dismissal paths (ESC, overlay click, the DialogContent X wired through onOpenChange) invoke neither onEnable nor resetState. A user who dismisses the backup-codes dialog with ESC or the X leaves the security settings page showing 2FA as disabled even though the server has it enabled (stale until a full page refresh), and the one-time-displayed backup codes are dismissed without copy/download with no way to view them again short of disabling and re-enabling 2FA.

adjudication.rationale: In EnableTwoFactorModal, handleEnable’s 200-success path was changed from `onEnable()` to `setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes)` (diff shows this at `if (response.status === 200) { setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes); return; }`). The only place that now calls `onEnable()` is the DisplayBackupCodes step’s “close” button handler, which also calls `resetState()`. However, the Dialog is controlled via `<Dialog open={open} onOpenChange={onOpenChange}>` and there is no wrapper that calls `resetState()` or `onEnable()` when the dialog is dismissed via ESC/overlay click/“X” (i.e., via `onOpenChange`). So if a user dismisses the backup-codes step through those dialog dismissal paths, the parent callback previously used to update UI state won’t run, and the modal’s internal state also won’t be reset by this component. This is a behavior regression introduced by the diff and can plausibly leave the settings UI stale after 2FA is enabled on the server, while also letting users dismiss the one-time display of backup codes without copy/download.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Backup-code consumption in authorize() is a non-atomic read-modify-write: the encrypted list is decrypted, one entry nulled, and the entire list re-encrypted and written with no transaction, lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent sign-ins (double-submit, two devices, password-manager retry) both read the same stored list and the second write clobbers the first, resurrecting a backup code the first request already consumed, and the same single-use code submitted twice inside the window grants two sessions — the use-exactly-once invariant the UI promises is silently broken.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` the backup-code path does a read-modify-write without any transactional/conditional protection: it decrypts `user.backupCodes`, finds `index`, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then `await prisma.user.update({ data: { backupCodes: symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), ...) }})`. Two concurrent sign-ins using the same backup code can both read the same original encrypted list before either write commits, both pass the `index !== -1` check, and both then write back an updated list—allowing the same single-use code to authenticate twice and potentially clobbering each other’s updates. The diff itself promises single-use codes in UI text (`backup_code_instructions`), so this is a correctness/security defect exposed by the new logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The backup-code branch parses the credential store with an unguarded JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)) directly in the request handler. When CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY has been rotated since the codes were stored (or the column is corrupt), symmetricDecrypt throws a decryption error or returns garbage and JSON.parse throws SyntaxError, escaping as an unhandled 500 HTML response from an endpoint whose contract returns 400 JSON for every other failure; the client's response.json() then rejects and the user sees only a generic error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds backup-code flows that decrypt and JSON.parse stored backup codes without guarding against decrypt/parse failures. In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts`, the backup-code branch does `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` with no try/catch around it. Similarly, in `packages/features/auth/lib/next-auth-options.ts` the backup-code login path does the same unguarded decrypt+parse. If the ciphertext is invalid (e.g., corruption or key rotation), `symmetricDecrypt` and/or `JSON.parse` can throw and escape the normal `{ error: ... }` JSON contract, leading to a 500 response that callers like `DisableTwoFactorModal` will attempt `response.json()` on and fail.
